lens: The coexistence of hormetic dose-response patterns across phylogenetically distant species—from GA3 in wasps to fibrates in C. elegans—suggests a universal stress-adaptation mechanism, while the stark contrast between strong genetic longevity signals (e.g., FOXO3 SNPs) and low population heritability in humans reveals a critical gap in understanding cohort-specific epigenetic modulation.
known_to_ignore: Genetic factors influence lifespan variation in model organisms
Environmental and dietary interventions can extend lifespan in short-lived species
Heritability estimates for complex traits are context-dependent
tensions: In parasitoid wasps, GA3 increases longevity at 50-200 ppm but decreases at 2000 ppm (fact_id=60218), whereas in C. elegans, fibrates extend lifespan at 10 μM without reported high-dose harm (fact_id=60906), challenging the universality of hormetic dose thresholds across taxa.

Heritability of human longevity is below 10% in historical cohorts (fact_id=2885), yet genetic enrichment in offspring reduces mortality by 30% (fact_id=10028), indicating that genetic signals may be masked or amplified by cohort-specific environmental or epigenetic factors.
gaps: Dose-response relationships for anti-aging compounds (e.g., oleuropein, fibrates) in mammalian models, particularly primates, where only correlative genetic data exist (fact_id=27050).
The role of Nrf2-signaling regulators (Keap1, βTrCP) in longevity beyond rodent species (fact_id=3432, fact_id=3431), with no data on human or primate tissues.
Epigenetic mechanisms (e.g., DNA methylation) underlying the low heritability of longevity in human cohorts, specifically in early 20th-century birth groups (fact_id=2885).

theses.title: Cross-Species Hormesis in Longevity Interventions: A Meta-Analysis of Biphasic Dose-Responses
theses.rationale: Synthesizes dose-response data from wasps (GA3), C. elegans (oleuropein, fibrates), and insects (UV-A exposure) to test for consistent hormetic thresholds, addressing safety implications for human anti-aging therapies.

theses.title: Epigenetic Modulation of Genetic Longevity Signals: Resolving the Heritability Paradox in Historical Human Cohorts
theses.rationale: Proposes that DNA methylation (fact_id=3160) and cohort-specific environments explain why genetic enrichment studies show strong effects (fact_id=10028) while population heritability remains low (fact_id=2885), guiding future longitudinal epigenomic studies.

reviewer_objections: For the hormesis thesis: Pharmacokinetic differences across species may invalidate direct dose comparisons, and mechanisms like GA3 signaling in wasps may not translate to mammalian systems.

For the heritability thesis: Low heritability in historical cohorts could reflect poor data quality or survivorship bias, and genetic enrichment studies may involve select families not representative of general populations.
next_extractions: Dose-response data for Nrf2-pathway activators (e.g., sulforaphane) in primate cell cultures or mouse models with varying maximum lifespan.
Epigenetic clocks and DNA methylation patterns in human cohorts with birth years from 1900-1950, correlated with longevity and genetic risk variants (e.g., FOXO3 SNPs from fact_id=5979).
